policies.summary: For a facility that needs a state certificate (25 MW or more, or storage of 25 MWh or more), failing city, county or airport zoning does not stop the Commission from issuing it, and once it issues no city, county or regulatory agency may require any further approval, permit or license for construction.

A generating plant or group of plants at a single site totaling 25 MW or more, or an electric storage unit of 25 MWh or more, needs a certificate of public convenience, use and necessity from the Iowa Utilities Commission; smaller facilities need no Commission certificate and are left to county and city zoning.

restrictions.description: Proposed 765 kV MISO transmission line, land negotiations in the Hebron area, and concern that data centers require large amounts of electricity and water. Active as of 2026-09-23. On Sept. 9, 2026 the Board repealed and rescinded Resolution No. 2026-45 (the Adair County Data Center Regulatory Ordinance) because the required public hearing had not yet been held; that did not affect the Resolution #2026-26 moratorium. A public hearing on the data center regulatory ordinance was set for 9:15 a.m. on 2026-09-23; its outcome was not yet reported at research time. The Board also set a $500 data center permit fee in August 2026. Legal basis: Resolution #2026-26, "Resolution to Establish a Temporary Moratorium on the Construction of Data Centers, High-Density Computing Facilities, and Battery Storage Facilities in the Unincorporated Areas of Adair County, Iowa," adopted March 18, 2026 by unanimous 5-0 roll call.

restrictions.description: County regulations were silent on digital asset mining, cryptocurrency operations, data processing centers, and battery/energy storage uses. Active as of 2026-09-23. Extended via Resolution #26-69 (adopted 2026-03-17) through 2027-03-31, covering digital asset mining, cryptocurrency operations, and data processing centers (BESS was moved to permanent Ordinance No. 330, adopted the same day). No further rescission or replacement found; a September 2026 statewide roundup still lists the moratorium as in place through March 2027. Legal basis: Resolution #25-97 (adopted 2025-06-17); extended via Resolution #26-36 (adopted 2025-11-25) through 2026-03-31; further extended via Resolution #26-69 (adopted 2026-03-17) through 2027-03-31. The same March 17, 2026 meeting adopted Ordinance No. 330 (third consideration), which permanently regulates battery/energy storage uses, spinning BESS out of the moratorium; the moratorium itself continues to cover digital asset mining, cryptocurrency operations, and data processing centers.

Concentrating solar power is prohibited, and fenced arrays over 160 acres need a wildlife corridor.
restrictions.long_description: setback: solar panels, structures and electrical equipment (excluding fences and interconnection lines) 300 ft from dwellings unless the owner waives it in writing (recorded); 120 ft from the centerline of perennial stream corridors and open ditches; 50 ft from property lines in the Renewable Energy overlay district (may be reduced to zero next to another overlay use). Battery energy storage: 200 ft from a property line or right-of-way; 500 ft from the nearest property line including an occupied structure off the subject property, reducible to 200 ft by a recorded, notarized waiver from that owner; 120 ft from perennial stream corridors and open ditches; sited inside a new solar facility when built with one. overlay_zone: rezoning to the Renewable Energy overlay district and the minimum passing threshold on the Linn County Utility Scale Solar Scorecard. noise_limit: hourly average 55 dBA by day (sunrise to sunset) and 50 dBA at night (sunset to sunrise) at the occupied dwelling of an adjacent residential property, or ambient Leq plus 5 dBA where ambient is higher; neighbours may waive in writing. Other: concentrating solar power (CSP) systems prohibited; fenced array areas over 160 acres require a wildlife corridor; panels at least 24 in. above ground at maximum tilt.

restrictions.long_description: On September 24, 2024, Clinton County’s Planning and Zoning Commission issued a three-month moratorium on commercial wind farm applications as they revised the county’s 2008 wind ordinance. This moratorium was extended in December 2024 and will run through June 2025. A community opposition group, Clinton & Jackson County Iowa Residents Against Wind Turbines, has collected over 700 signatures for a petition against the project and has been active in public hearings regarding the proposed ordinance. [Note: As of January 2025, the proposed ordinance from the County Commission leaves little land available for commercial wind. The required setbacks for wind would be 5 miles in either direction from byway roads, 1,500 feet from property lines, and two miles from any incorporated city. A proposed wind project from NextEra Energy, which would have a capacity of 250 MW, would most likely be held back if the county supervisors approved the commission’s updated ordinance.]

projects.description: In August 2018, the Madison County Coalition for Scenic Preservation challenged Madison County’s decision to approve this 52-turbine wind farm.
projects.long_description: In August 2018, the Madison County Coalition for Scenic Preservation challenged Madison County’s decision to approve this 52-turbine wind farm. In June 2019 the district court dismissed the case and the plaintiffs appealed; the Iowa Court of Appeals affirmed the lower court in January 2021. However, in December 2020, Madison County adopted an ordinance capping the number of turbines in the county at the current number, effectively preventing the project from proceeding. In January 2021, MidAmerican sued the county, and in March 2022, the parties reached a settlement allowing the company to construct 30 turbines. However, in July 2022, MidAmerican abandoned plans to move forward with the project, due to the reduction in size, among other issues.

projects.description: Beginning in 2019, the developer of Coggon Solar began public outreach related to an application for a 640-acre, 100-MW solar project in Linn County.
projects.long_description: Beginning in 2019, the developer of Coggon Solar began public outreach related to an application for a 640-acre, 100-MW solar project in Linn County. After residents voiced opposition to taking farmland out of commission, the Planning & Zoning Commission voted to recommend that the County Board of Supervisors deny the project. In January 2022, the Board voted 2-1 to approve the project. However, a family who lives near the proposed project brought a lawsuit against the board of supervisors, and, in July 2022, the Iowa Utilities Board denied Coggon Solar’s request for a certificate while the lawsuit was ongoing. On or before February 1, 2023, the court dismissed the lawsuit against the board of supervisors, paving the way for the project to move forward.

projects.description: In 2022, Palo-area residents filed a lawsuit opposing the rezoning of land for two industrial-scale solar projects, claiming that the Linn County Board of Supervisors failed to follow county land-use policies and relied on illegal spot zoning to permit a renewable energy project near the decommissioned Duane Arnold nuclear plant.
projects.long_description: In 2022, Palo-area residents filed a lawsuit opposing the rezoning of land for two industrial-scale solar projects, claiming that the Linn County Board of Supervisors failed to follow county land-use policies and relied on illegal spot zoning to permit a renewable energy project near the decommissioned Duane Arnold nuclear plant. A judge denied the claims in July 2023, pointing to the fact that the town’s Comprehensive Plan promotes the “protection and enhancement of the health and safety of all Linn County residents through the use of renewable energy.”

projects.description: A 3-turbine wind farm that was approved in 2015 and then constructed was taken down in 2018 following a successful legal challenge by residents.
projects.long_description: A 3-turbine wind farm that was approved in 2015 and then constructed was taken down in 2018 following a successful legal challenge by residents. On appeal, the Court of Appeals of Iowa affirmed the judgment of the Iowa District Court for Fayette County that wind turbines were not “electrical and natural gas transmission and regulating facilities” within the meaning of the relevant county ordinance and thus a special permit was required for them to be placed on agricultural land.

projects.description: In August 2015, the Black Hawk County Board of Adjustment unanimously voted to deny a special permit and setback variance for Optimum Renewables’ proposed 3-turbine, 6-MW wind energy project.
projects.long_description: In August 2015, the Black Hawk County Board of Adjustment unanimously voted to deny a special permit and setback variance for Optimum Renewables’ proposed 3-turbine, 6-MW wind energy project. The decision effectively ended plans for the project in Black Hawk County, which would have been the county’s first wind farm. Roughly fifty project opponents attended the board’s meeting and expressed concerns about potential impacts to wildlife, livestock, property values, and human health. Optimum then sought to build the project in the neighboring Buchanan County. The project also met local opposition in Buchanan County, where residents expressed concerns about the project’s potential impacts to local livelihoods and voiced skepticism about promises made by project advocates. In August 2015, the Buchanan County Planning and Zoning Commission denied a rezoning application that would have allowed Optimum Renewables to build a wind farm in the county. The project was finally built in Fayette County in 2016. Opposition continued from Fayette residents, including the group Fairbank Citizens Against Industrial Wind Turbines Near Our City, who claimed that the project violated county zoning laws. In November 2016, an Iowa judge held that the project was illegal and void due to zoning violations, issuing an order requiring its removal. In May 2018, the Iowa Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal of the decision, effectively ending the project.

projects.description: In October 2023, the Dickinson County Board of Adjustment denied Invenergy a permit to proceed with a proposed 79-turbine wind farm in Dickinson County.
projects.long_description: In October 2023, the Dickinson County Board of Adjustment denied Invenergy a permit to proceed with a proposed 79-turbine wind farm in Dickinson County. The project will have a total capacity of 300 MW, including two additional phases in Emmet and Clay Counties (see entry on Emmet County). The Board’s 3-day hearing gathered input from those in favor of and opposed to the project, including members of Dickinson County Concerned Citizens, an organization staunchly opposed to the Redrock Wind Energy Center. In April 2024, the developer met with the county to discuss a proposal for a pared down version of the project. In May 2025, after three days of public hearings, the Dickinson County Board of Adjustment voted unanimously to approve the conditional use permit for a revised version of the proposal with 64 wind turbines.

projects.description: In August 2022, a local resident involved with Tama County Against Turbines Coalition filed a petition for declaratory judgment that the conditional use permits issued by the Tama County Board of Adjustment to Salt Creek Wind were illegal.
projects.long_description: In August 2022, a local resident involved with Tama County Against Turbines Coalition filed a petition for declaratory judgment that the conditional use permits issued by the Tama County Board of Adjustment to Salt Creek Wind were illegal. Two months earlier, in June 2022, another member of the same group filed a lawsuit against the board for failing to vote on a moratorium on wind energy and for readopting the existing wind ordinance without following proper procedures. The June 2022 case was dismissed in October 2022. At a public meeting in December 2022, several residents urged the board to adopt a 6-month or 12-month moratorium. In April 2023, Salt Creek Wind, LLC sued Tama County Against Turbines and several of its individual members, claiming that the group had “chastised and bullied the [Board of] Supervisors [to] issue a moratorium on wind energy projects” and had “filed frivolous lawsuits . . . to frustrate . . . contracts between Salt Creek and the local landowners.” Also in April 2023, Southern Natural Resources, LLC (SNR) sued Salt Creek Wind, LLC and associated companies, alleging that the development was in violation of SNR’s exclusive development rights in the area and that the project misappropriated proprietary and trade secret information.

projects.description: In August 2022, the Page County Board of Supervisors approved the 200-MW Shenandoah Hills Wind Farm after 6 months of opposition from residents, who raised concerns about setbacks, noise, lighting, and decommissioning agreements.
projects.long_description: In August 2022, the Page County Board of Supervisors approved the 200-MW Shenandoah Hills Wind Farm after 6 months of opposition from residents, who raised concerns about setbacks, noise, lighting, and decommissioning agreements. Just over a month after the approval, residents opposed to the project filed a lawsuit against the county and board in state court, which was later removed to federal court. In February 2023, after the developer, Invenergy, informed the Board of Supervisors that it would be removing 3 turbines from the plan, the Page County Zoning Administrator informed the developer that this was a “material change,” which rendered the application “void” and revoked the permit. The developer appealed the Zoning Administrator’s decision to the Page County Board of Adjustment. In March 2023, the Board of Adjustment upheld the revocation of the permit. A week later, the developer filed a lawsuit against the County officials in federal court challenging the revocation. In May 2024, the federal court denied the residents’ state claims which had been rendered moot at the time the permit was revoked. In November 2024, in a 2-1 vote, the Board of Supervisors approved a resolution to enter into a settlement agreement resolving the pending litigation and allowing the developer to proceed with construction of the project. In November 2025, construction of the project was completed, and the facility began operating with a total of 54 wind turbines and a generating capacity of 214 MW.

projects.long_description: Local residents have expressed opposition to MidAmerican’s proposal to construct a 400-MW, 140-turbine wind farm in northern Mills and southern Pottawattamie counties. As of February 8, 2023, over 1,100 people had joined a private Facebook group called “Say NO to the Silver Creek Wind Farm.”

projects.description: The viability of MidAmerican Energy’s plans to construct the 90-turbine Siouxland Wind Farm is in doubt due to Woodbury County’s adoption of an ordinance in August 2022 that increased the setback distance from wind turbines to occupied residences from 1,250 feet to 2,500 feet.
projects.long_description: The viability of MidAmerican Energy’s plans to construct the 90-turbine Siouxland Wind Farm is in doubt due to Woodbury County’s adoption of an ordinance in August 2022 that increased the setback distance from wind turbines to occupied residences from 1,250 feet to 2,500 feet. As described above, the ordinance reduced the buildable acres in the county from 177 to 1.7. Opponents of the project cited noise and visual impacts, and over 700 residents signed a petition to increase the setback distance. Opponents of the project are seeking further changes to the ordinances regulating wind turbines, up to and including a ban on wind farms, and have stated that “[MidAmerican] just need[s] to pack up and go somewhere else where it’s more suitable.” MidAmerican is still looking to move forward with this project despite heavy resistance and ordinance changes.

projects.description: In 2024, Invenergy proposed the Red Rock Wind Energy Center with a total capacity of 300 MW, two be developed in phases on property in Emmet, Dickinson, Clay Counties (see entry on Dickinson County).
projects.long_description: In 2024, Invenergy proposed the Red Rock Wind Energy Center with a total capacity of 300 MW, two be developed in phases on property in Emmet, Dickinson, Clay Counties (see entry on Dickinson County). In October 2024, the Emmet County Board of Adjustment denied a conditional use permit for the phase of the project in Emmet County. In December 2024, the developer filed a lawsuit against the Board of Adjustment alleging that the denial was in bad faith as the project proposal was not subject to the 2024 moratorium halting the issuance of conditional use permits for wind projects that the county adopted within days of its application. The developer asserts that its permit application complies with the requirements of the 2011 ordinance regulating wind projects in the county. As of November 2025, the developer and the Emmet County Board of Supervisors were negotiating a settlement agreement to resolve the pending lawsuit and approve the conditional use permit for the project, subject to the terms and conditions in the agreement.
